fields.title: Panamá: Terremoto en Azuero y Veraguas - Informe de Situación No. 01 (al 10 de octubre 2026, 13:15)
fields.body:
**DESTACADOS**

- El 9 de octubre a las 12:56 p.m. un **sismo de magnitud** 7.2 (según el Instituto de Geociencias de la Universidad de Panamá, IGC-UP) se registró a 39 km al noroeste de Tonosí en la provincia sur-central de Los Santos y a 4 km de profundidad. La secuencia **sigue activa**, con 56 réplicas registradas hasta las 8:11 p.m. No se reportan víctimas mortales ni personas desaparecidas.
- El 10 de octubre el Consejo de Gabinete, convocado por Presidencia, declara estado de emergencia tras el terremoto ocurrido en el país este 9 de octubre.
- El Sistema Nacional de Protección Civil (SINAPROC) reportó **al menos 134 viviendas afectadas, 27 personas con lesiones y 188 centros educativos con daños** a nivel nacional a las 8:00p.m.
- **Las provincias de Veraguas, Coclé, Los Santos y Herrera** concentran la mayoría de los daños. En Veraguas, los corregimientos de Arena, Cacao y Quebro siguen **incomunicados** y hay interrupciones de electricidad, agua potable e internet.
- Unas **300 personas fueron evacuadas** de Isla Cañas (Los Santos) por el aumento del nivel del mar, y **ocho familias** están en un albergue habilitado en Penonomé (Coclé).
- El Ministerio de Salud (MINSA) reportó 17 instalaciones de salud afectadas con daños no estructurales: 6 hospitales, 8 centros de salud y 3 MINSA-CAPSI (Centros de Atención Primaria en Salud Innovadores). Se registraron evacuaciones en hospitales de Los Santos, Chiriquí, Herrera y la región metropolitana. En el Hospital del Oriente Chiricano (209 personas) se registró una evacuación total.
- El Ministerio de Educación (MEDUCA) suspendió las clases a nivel nacional y reportó 188 centros educativos afectados. Entre los centros educativos con afectaciones en la infraestructura se encuentran 22 en la Comarca indígena Ngäbe-Buglé, 15 en Chiriquí, 5 en Panamá Centro, 4 en Los Santos y 3 en Panamá Este. En la Escuela Alberto Zúñiga (Coclé) se reportaron 15 estudiantes con lesiones menores.
- El Instituto de Acueductos y Alcantarillados Nacionales (IDAAN) informó que la potabilizadora de Chilibre opera al 100% y que el suministro se recupera progresivamente.

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: Panama: Earthquake in Azuero & Veraguas - Situation Report No. 01 (as of 10 October 2026, 13:15)
fields.body:
**KEY POINTS**

- On 9 October at 12:56 p.m., a **magnitude 7.2 earthquake** struck 39 km north-west of Tonosí, in the south-central province of Los Santos, at a depth of 4 km, according to the University of Panama’s Institute of Geosciences (IGC-UP). **Aftershocks are ongoing**, with 56 aftershocks recorded up to 8:11 p.m. No deaths or missing people have been reported.
- On 10 October, the Cabinet Council, convened by the President of Panama, declared a state of emergency following the earthquake.
- The National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) reported **at least 134 damaged homes, 27 people injured and 188 damaged schools** nationwide as of 8:00 p.m.
- **Veraguas, Coclé, Los Santos and Herrera provinces** account for most of the damage. In Veraguas, the townships (*corregimientos*) of Arena, Cacao and Quebro remain **cut off**, with power, water and Internet outages.
- Some **300 people were evacuated** from Isla Cañas (Los Santos) due to rising sea levels, and **eight families** are staying in a shelter set up in Penonomé (Coclé).
- The Ministry of Health (MINSA) reported non-structural damage to 17 health facilities: 6 hospitals, 8 health centres and 3 MINSA-CAPSI (Innovative Primary Health Care Centres). Hospitals in Los Santos, Chiriquí and Herrera provinces and the Panama City metropolitan area were evacuated, and the Hospital del Oriente Chiricano was fully evacuated (209 people).
- The Ministry of Education (MEDUCA) suspended classes nationwide and reported 188 affected schools. Those with infrastructure damage include 22 in the Ngäbe-Buglé Indigenous *comarca* (a semi-autonomous territory), 15 in Chiriquí, 5 in Panamá Centro, 4 in Los Santos and 3 in Panamá Este. At the Alberto Zúñiga School (Coclé), 15 students suffered minor injuries.
- The National Institute of Aqueducts and Sewers (IDAAN) reported that the Chilibre water treatment plant is operating at full capacity and that supply is gradually recovering.

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: PANAMÁ: Terremoto - Flash Update No. 01 al 9 de octubre de 2026
fields.body:
**DESTACADOS**

- Un terremoto de magnitud 7.7 (GDACS) y con profundidad de 10 km sacudió Panamá a las 12:56 p.m. hora local el 9 de octubre, con epicentro en la península de Azuero en el sur del istmo, a unos 39 km al oeste de Tonosí (provincia de Los Santos).
- A la hora de corte se han registrado más de 40 réplicas, varias con magnitudes superiores a 5.5. Se levantó la alerta de tsunami.
- No hay reporte oficial de personas afectadas. El Sistema Nacional de protección Civil (SINAPROC) informa que en las provincias de Coclé, Veraguas y Los Santos hay afectaciones en edificaciones gubernamentales, comercios privados y daños en infraestructuras viales. Se registraron evacuaciones masivas de edificios a nivel nacional.
- No hay solicitud de apoyo internacional.

**RESUMEN DE LA SITUACIÓN**

- El 9 de octubre, aproximadamente a las 12:56 pm hora local, un fuerte sismo sacudió Panamá. El Global Disaster Awareness and Coordination System (GDACS) reporta una magnitud de 7.7 a poca profundidad (10 km), con epicentro en la península sur-central de Azuero. El sismo se sintió con fuerza en la capital y en las provincias centrales, y a la hora de corte se habían registrado más de 40 réplicas, varias de ellas con magnitudes superiores a 5.5 y una máxima de 6.9, según el Instituto de Geociencias de la Universidad de Panamá.
- No hay reportes de víctimas, pero se han reportado daños en edificios y carreteras. Se emitió, y luego se levantó, un aviso de tsunami para las zonas costeras del Pacífico. Las autoridades nacionales han hecho un llamado a las comunidades costeras para que se alejen de la orilla. El Aeropuerto Internacional de Tocumen, ubicado en la capital, suspendió las operaciones aéreas por varias horas antes de reanudarlas. Se informa que el Canal de Panamá opera con normalidad.
- El Instituto Nacional de Acueductos y Alcantarillados Nacionales (IDAAN) informa que varias plantas potabilizadoras a nivel nacional presentan interrupciones o reducciones en su producción, debido a fallas eléctricas relacionadas con la situación sísmica registrada. Entre las instalaciones se encuentra la Potabilizadora Federico Guardia Conte (Chilibre), operando al 20% de su capacidad de producción.
- El Ministerio de Educación, la Universidad de Panamá, la Universidad Tecnológica de Panamá y la Universidad Católica Santa María la Antigua de Panamá suspendieron las clases de la tarde y las actividades de sus oficinas administrativas en todo el país.
- La respuesta está liderada por el Gobierno de Panamá a través del Sistema Nacional de Protección Civil (SINAPROC) y el Centro de Operaciones de Emergencia (COE), organismo adscrito al SINAPROC. A la hora de corte no se ha recibido solicitud de asistencia internacional.
- El Sistema de las Naciones Unidas en Panamá está movilizado y en contacto directo con el Gobierno. Se activo el Grupo de Respuesta de Emergencia de Naciones Unidas y se mantiene preparado para apoyar a las autoridades según sea necesario.

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: Attacks on Health Care in Myanmar: 16-30 September 2026
fields.body:
Data collected by Insecurity Insight shows that since the military coup on 01 February 2021 and 31 August 2026, at least [**1,973 incidents**](https://us.list-manage.com/V2Rkb0R_W6e?e=e2fc04a6ae&c2id=2821d00d2df9cfdc1e0140433e086a6f) of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across Myanmar:

- **health facilities were damaged 519 times**
- **175 health workers were killed, 940 arrested and 55 kidnapped**

Since January 2025, incidents involving damage to or destruction of temporary or makeshift health facilities in Myanmar have increased sharply, from four incidents between February 2021 and December 2024 to 33 between January 2025 and August 2026. In total, 89% of the reported incidents were attributed to Myanmar Armed Forces (MAF) aircraft and drone strikes. Temporary or makeshift health facilities in Sagaing Region were particularly affected, with incidents also frequently reported in Kachin and Mandalay.

**Documented incidents**

**16-30 September 2026**

The publicly reported incidents below are not a complete nor a representative list of all incidents that affected the provision of health care in Myanmar between 16-30 September 2026. The incidents have not been verified through ground investigations. There is a delay in reporting incidents due to our open-source verification protocol.  
  
**22 September 2026:** In Hakha town, Hakha township and district, Chin state, a hospital came under attack when seven gunmen opened fire with small firearms and mortars. Junta security forces returned fire. The attack occurred during a blood donation ceremony organised by members of the junta police force at the hospital. Junta authorities accused the Chin Defence Force (CDF) of carrying out the attack. **Sources:** [**Myanmar Digital News**](https://us.list-manage.com/LYlB_h2KX0K?e=e2fc04a6ae&c2id=2821d00d2df9cfdc1e0140433e086a6f) **and** [**People Media**](https://us.list-manage.com/YowAcKKo3F0?e=e2fc04a6ae&c2id=2821d00d2df9cfdc1e0140433e086a6f)  
  
**As reported on 28 September 2026:** In Natogyi and Taungtha townships, Myingyan district, Mandalay region, the Myanmar military banned the transportation of medicines and food from towns to villages from early September 2026. Following an attack on a military airport in Tada-U township on 10 September, the blockade was further reinforced. **Source:** [**Mandalay Free Press**](https://us.list-manage.com/anSu7YD8oqa?e=e2fc04a6ae&c2id=2821d00d2df9cfdc1e0140433e086a6f)

fields.title: Pakistan Weekly Market Monitor Report - 1 October 2025
fields.body:
- The cost of staple food (wheat flour, cooking oil, and pulses) remained 14.2 percent above its level before the Middle East conflict, as of 1 October, reflecting a combination of domestic market factors and higher fuel and import costs.
- Wheat flour prices marginally increased (0.3%) during the week, however, remained 19 percent above pre-conflict levels.
- The cost of basic food basket1 for a six-member household stood at PKR 17,300 per month (USD 62.5), equivalent to PKR 4,325 per week (USD 15.6) nationwide, excluding lower cost items such as vegetables or spices.
- Petrol and diesel prices remain 50 percent and 45 percent above pre-conflict levels despite recent declines.
- Regional energy and shipping disruptions continue to push up prices in domestic markets.
- Food price pressures persist despite stable commodity availability across markets.

fields.title: Protection Cluster: West Bank Operational Update | 1 June - 31 August 2026
fields.body:
**Protection Developments – Escalating Settler Violence and Displacement**

Between June and August 2026, the operating environment in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, deteriorated further amid a worsening security situation and additional measures by Israeli authorities that constrained humanitarian access and operations.  
 During the reporting period, OHCHR verified the killing of 27 Palestinians in the West Bank, including eight boys. Of these, 20 were killed by Israeli forces (IF), two by Israeli settlers, and five by either IF or Israeli settlers. In addition, two Israelis, including one civilian and one IF member, were killed in settler attacks followed by clashes with Palestinians.  
 Settler violence continued to intensify in scale, geographic spread, and severity, with repeated attacks occurring amid persistent impunity and insufficient protection for affected Palestinian communities. OCHA recorded 229 settler attacks resulting in casualties and/or property damage in June 2026, 221 in July, and 198 in August, up from 148 in January 2026, reflecting a sustained upward trend. Annual incidents have exceeded 1,000 since 2023 and reached 1,836 in 2025. In many cases, attacks reportedly occurred in the presence of IF, which are increasingly seen failing to prevent, facilitating, or participating in such violence.

A related trend was the expansion of settler attacks beyond areas qualified as “C” under the Oslo Accords, alongside the growth of settler farm outposts, which reportedly controlled about 18% of West Bank land as of July 2026. According to the CSO Yesh Din, the share of attacks occurring in Areas “A” and “B” increased from 32% in 2025 to 63% in January-June 2026. This surge contributed to increased casualties, property damage and livelihood losses, movement restrictions, limited access to services, heightened displacement risks, shrinking safe spaces for Palestinians, and increasingly constrained humanitarian operations.

In one particularly grave incident, on 24 July 2026, approximately 60 settlers, several of them armed, entered the village of Tell, southwest of Nablus in Area “B”, reportedly as part of an unauthorized hike, triggering clashes involving Palestinians, armed settlers, and IF. Four Palestinian men from the same family and two Israelis, one of them an off duty IF soldier, were killed. The incident was followed by what appeared to be extensive collective punishment measures, including the temporary detention of approximately 100 Palestinian men. In the following days, settlers carried out coordinated attacks across Qalqilya and Nablus in apparent retaliation, resulting in Palestinian injuries, extensive property damage, and movement restrictions that impeded access to essential services. According to the CSO Peace Now, settlers had established five outposts near Tell in reprisal by the end of July.

A similar incident occurred on 21 August 2026 in Sa'ir, Hebron (also in Area “B”), when at least 50 settlers participating in a reported unauthorized hike entered the village armed with firearms, batons, sharp objects, slings, and Molotov cocktails. They attacked homes and residents, resulting in the shooting and killing of a 16-year-old boy and critically injuring several others, including a 71-year-old man.

A related emerging pattern involved the forcible displacement of Palestinian families from homes in residential areas on the outskirts of Palestinian villages in Area “B”, following sustained harassment and intimidation by Israeli settlers. In several cases, families reportedly endured prolonged sieges of their homes, including repeated attacks and obstruction of access to essential services and supplies, making daily life untenable and ultimately forcing them to leave. Their properties were subsequently occupied by settlers.

One such incident occurred on 22 July 2026, when two Palestinian families comprising seven people, including three children, were displaced from their home northeast of Jalud, Nablus, following months of settler violence and harassment. After a nearby outpost was established in April, the families reportedly faced repeated attacks, had their vehicle burned, were denied access to food and medicine, and experienced disruptions to water and electricity services. Settlers reportedly occupied the two homes immediately after the families left.

A similar case occurred in Area B near Qusra, Nablus Governorate. On 9 August 2026, settlers from a nearby outpost blocked access roads to three Palestinian homes and erected a tent between them, effectively trapping approximately 15 Palestinians, including children, inside. Although Israeli forces later removed the tent, deployed to the area and declared it a closed military zone, residents continued to face severe movement restrictions as of the end of August, with limited access to food, water and other essential supplies. Settler harassment and intimidation continued, while visits to the affected homes required prior coordination with the Israeli military.

Against this backdrop, protection partners faced growing challenges in addressing protection risks and maintaining services to affected communities. Reports indicated increased harassment and attacks against humanitarian actors, which, together with the designation of some affected areas as closed military zones, further restricted humanitarian space.

fields.title: Dooplaya District Incident Report: Burma Army shelling injured three villagers and damaged a house in Waw Ray Township (June 2026)
fields.body: *This Incident Report describes events occurring in Waw Ray (Win Yay) Township, Dooplaya District, in June 2026. On 21 June 2026, Burma Army soldiers based in Ac--- army camp, Ac--- village, Noh Shoo Neh village tract, Waw Ray Township, fired two mortar shells, and one of the shells landed next to a villager’s house, injuring three villagers and damaging the house and some plantations in Aa--- village, Win Hk’Na village tract, Waw Ray Township. Due to this shelling, some students were afraid to go to school, and the villagers had to work in fear. Some of the students also suffered from malaria and could not go to school.*[*\[1\]*](https://khrg.org/2026/10/26-192-i1/dooplaya-district-incident-report-burma-army-shelling-injured-three-villagers-and#ftn1)

fields.title: Lebanon: Minutes of Meeting - Inter-Sector Coordination Group Meeting - 2 October 2026
fields.body:
**1. Opening Remarks**  
  
Dr. Ola Boutros, LRP General Supervisor (MoSA)  
Stephanie Laba, ISCG Co-Chair (UNHCR)  
Kiri Ginnerup, ISCG Co-Chair OIC (UNDP)  
Rana El Khawand, ISCG Co-Chair OIC (OCHA)  
  
The Inter-Sector Coordination Group (ISCG) Co-Chairs welcomed participants to the October ISCG meeting and noted the shift of the ISCG meetings to an in-person modality, with limited exceptions for colleagues unable to attend in person, including those outside Lebanon and Operational Coordination Group (OCG) Co-Chairs. The shift is intended to facilitate more meaningful discussion and interaction among members. New colleagues were invited to introduce themselves, including Rana El Khawand, representing OCHA as ISCG Co-Chair; Kiri Ginnerup, representing UNDP as ISCG Co-Chair; and Farah Ismail, Protection Sector NGO Co-Coordinator from OXFAM. The ISCG Co-Chairs also presented the action points and the meeting agenda.  
  
Dr. Ola Boutros acknowledged the considerable workload associated with this year’s two Flash Appeals and the LRP Addendum, as well as partners’ continued efforts to address related operational challenges. She welcomed the presentation of the Consolidation Plan by the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE) as an important step in moving the process forward. She noted that the Ministry of Social Affairs (MoSA) continues to closely monitor the situation in Tyre in coordination with the Disaster Risk Management (DRM) unit and is working to facilitate cash-for-rent assistance for vulnerable families in the Bekaa. She concluded by encouraging active engagement in the upcoming Lebanon Response Plan (LRP) 2027 Planning and Needs Analysis Workshop on 16 October.

fields.title: UNRWA Situation Report #236 on the Humanitarian Crisis in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem [EN/AR]
fields.body:
**Highlights**

The Gaza Strip

- Over 106,000 children attended in-person learning in UNRWA Temporary Learning Spaces (TLS) during the first weeks of the 2026/2027 school year, marking an important milestone in efforts to expand access to learning across the Gaza Strip. At the same time, demand for in-person learning continues to outpace available capacity, and efforts are ongoing to identify additional learning spaces and expand existing TLS. Learning activities continue in challenging conditions in many locations, and significant investment is required to improve learning environments, undertake repairs, rehabilitate water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) facilities, and produce essential education furniture. UNRWA estimates that several million dollars are needed to address these requirements and support safe, inclusive, and conducive learning conditions for children across UNRWA schools and temporary learning spaces.
- Over the past months, with the support of partners, UNRWA teams have produced more than 6,000 pieces of furniture for UNRWA TLS and health centres, including desks, chairs, tables, cupboards, and benches, helping expand learning capacity despite severe resource constraints.
- Military activity remained concentrated along and around the Israeli-controlled military zone, known as the "Yellow Line", continuing to expose civilians to significant protection risks. UNRWA recorded several incidents affecting its installations and displaced persons sheltering within them. In the Middle Area, quadcopter fire prompted the precautionary relocation of displaced persons within an UNRWA school. In separate incidents in Jabalia, two displaced persons sheltering in UNRWA schools, including a seven-year-old child, were reportedly injured by gunfire while sleeping inside the shelters.
- As winter approaches, as [reported](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-2-october-2026) by the Site Management and Shelter Clusters, an estimated 235,000 people are sheltering in around 400 flood-prone displacement sites, while more than 44,000 people continue to live in unsafe buildings at heightened risk of collapse during winter. Combined, these figures represent over 13 per cent of Gaza's population exposed to heightened winter-related risks. On 28 September, the UN Humanitarian Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov [warned](https://dppa.un.org/en/speeches-and-statements/acting-special-coordinator-for-the-middle-east-peace-processs-remarks) the UN Security Council that “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items continue to impede the scale-up of the humanitarian response, including preparations” for the rainy season. As co-lead of the Site Management Cluster, UNRWA continues to coordinate and support winter preparedness and risk-reduction efforts through site-level risk assessments, prioritisation of high-risk locations, and coordination of targeted mitigation measures, including flood-risk reduction, access improvements, debris removal, site and shelter reinforcement, and community engagement.

**Key points**

The Gaza Strip

Fatalities and injuries

- Between 7 October 2023 and 2 October 2026, according to the Ministry of Health, as reported by the [Health Cluster](https://app.powerbi.com/view?r=eyJrIjoiODAxNTYzMDYtMjQ3YS00OTMzLTkxMWQtOTU1NWEwMzE5NTMwIiwidCI6ImY2MTBjMGI3LWJkMjQtNGIzOS04MTBiLTNkYzI4MGFmYjU5MCIsImMiOjh9&disablecdnExpiration=1780342572)[,](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/reported-impact-snapshot-gaza-strip-13-may-2026) 74,228 Palestinians were killed in the Gaza Strip and another 175,188 were injured. This includes 1,445 fatalities and 5,227 injuries between the announcement of a ceasefire agreement on 10 October 2025 and 2 October 2026.
- UNRWA has recorded 394 colleagues killed in the Gaza Strip since the start of the war (311 UNRWA personnel and 83 persons who were supporting UNRWA[\[2\]](https://www.unrwa.org/resources/reports/unrwa-situation-report-236-humanitarian-crisis-gaza-strip-and-occupied-west-bank#_ftn1), as of 6 October.

Health crisis

- The worsening fuel and engine oil shortage is increasingly disrupting health services across the Gaza Strip. The UN [warned](https://press.un.org/en/2026/db260917.doc.htm) that reduced fuel support to hospitals, driven by funding shortfalls and high procurement costs, could affect most hospitals and lead to cuts in primary and secondary healthcare services.
- In September, six UNRWA health centres also experienced temporary disruptions due to generator overload, highlighting the growing operational impact of the shortage of fuel, lubricant oil, and spare parts on the delivery of healthcare.

Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) needs

- According to the WASH Cluster’s [Light Touch Monitoring Survey](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/who-attacks-health-care-gaza-strip-1-january-2026-6-august-2026), completed in early July, 90 per cent of the population are experiencing frequent, unpredictable disruptions in access to safe, clean, and reliable water for daily drinking, cooking, and hygiene – an increase from 84 per cent the previous month.

Shelter needs

- According to the Shelter Cluster’s [classification](https://www.sheltercluster.org/palestine/documents/shelter-severity-and-household-needs-across-accessible-areas-gaza), based on surveys conducted between 14 and 28 June 2026, an estimated 1.98 million people, representing 94 per cent of the population of the Gaza Strip, require shelter and non-food item assistance (NFI). The assessment also suggests that 58 per cent of the population is facing critical or catastrophic shelter needs, meaning severe deficiencies in shelter conditions or lack of access to essential services and NFIs that expose them to serious health, safety, and dignity risks.

Operational implications and humanitarian response

- Around 10,500 Palestinian UNRWA personnel continue to provide services and assistance to people in the Gaza Strip. In the occupied West Bank, UNRWA also plays a central role with over 4,000 of the Agency’s Palestinian personnel providing education, health, and other services to Palestine Refugees.
- All UNRWA international staff are prevented from entering the Occupied Palestinian Territory - the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. This follows the implementation of laws passed by the Israeli parliament on 28 October 2024[\[3\]](https://www.unrwa.org/resources/reports/unrwa-situation-report-236-humanitarian-crisis-gaza-strip-and-occupied-west-bank#_ftn1) that purport to prohibit UNRWA’s operations in areas that Israel considers its sovereign territory, including occupied East Jerusalem, and seek to bar any contact between Israeli officials and UNRWA. **Israeli authorities have not granted the Agency’s international staff visas or permits to enter the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including the Gaza Strip, since the end of January 2025.**
- Since March 2025, the Israeli authorities have been blocking UNRWA from directly bringing humanitarian personnel and aid into the Gaza Strip. Despite the huge needs on the ground, UNRWA was therefore unable to distribute the aid it had pre-positioned outside Gaza, which included enough food parcels, flour, and shelter supplies for hundreds of thousands of people.

The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem

- According to [OCHA](https://www.ochaopt.org/data/casualties), between 7 October 2023 and 6 October 2026, 1,138 Palestinians – at least 250 of them children – were killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem. Ninety-one of them have been killed since the beginning of 2026.
- Israeli forces again renewed the military closure orders covering Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur Shams camps in the northern West Bank until 30 November, deepening the near-total restrictions on accessing the camps. Some 34,000 Palestine Refugees remain forcibly displaced as a result of the ongoing operation “Iron Wall”, which started in January 2025.
- Movement and access restrictions imposed by Israeli forces across the occupied West Bank were tightened during this period, coinciding with the Jewish holiday of Sukkot and in anticipation of the third anniversary of the attacks of 7 October 2023. The Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967 released [a statement](https://www.ohchr.org/en/press-releases/2026/10/checkpoints-occupied-west-bank-choking-palestinian-life-warns-un-expert) on 2 October condemning the impact of checkpoints on Palestinian life.
- Tendering for the construction of the E1 Israeli settlement plan located east of Jerusalem was postponed by the office of the Israeli Attorney General until after the upcoming Israeli elections. The E1 settlement project stands to displace multiple Palestine Refugee communities and would severely undermine the territorial contiguity of the occupied West Bank.
- During this period, two Palestinians were killed in connection with settler violence incidents, which also resulted in damage to Palestinian property and agricultural assets across the occupied West Bank. The official start of the annual olive harvest season is scheduled for 15 October, with an increase in settler violence and harassment anticipated.

fields.title: UNICEF Cameroon Cholera Outbreak Flash Update No. 4, 23 July-23 September 2026
fields.body:
**Highlights**

- The outbreak continues to expand geographically. Laboratory-confirmed cholera cases are reported in twenty-one health districts across the Far North and North regions, while four additional districts in the Far North remain under investigation for suspected cases.
- UNICEF is supporting the Government-led response through Health, WASH, Social and Behaviour Change, Accountability to Affected Populations, Child Protection, Nutrition, Youth Engagement and coordination.
- The response is 48 per cent funded. A US$660,800 gap remains, with particularly significant needs in Health, Nutrition and Child Protection/MHPSS.

**Overview**

Cholera transmission continues to expand across the Far North and North regions. Population movements and active transmission in neighbouring areas increase the risk of further spread. Immediate priorities include stronger surveillance, timely case management, targeted WASH interventions, risk communication and preparedness in affected and high-risk districts.

As of 23 September 2026, the Far North region has reported 2,753 cholera cases and 77 deaths (CFR: 2.8%), with active transmission persisting in several health districts, notably Mada, Kolofata, Mokolo, Mora and Makary. The implementation of two rounds of reactive Oral Cholera Vaccination (OCV) campaigns in seven high-risk districts (Fotokol, Kousseri, Mada, Makary, Mora, Kolofata and Mokolo) has likely contributed to reducing the spread and severity of the outbreak. However, the worsening humanitarian situation, including population displacement from Logone-et-Chari division due to insecurity, is placing additional pressure on host communities in Waza and the urban health districts of Maroua I, Maroua II and Maroua III. This influx of displaced populations is increasing vulnerability to cholera transmission through overcrowding and heightened pressure on already constrained health and WASH services.

In the North Region, 37 cases and 6 deaths have been reported (CFR: 16.22%). Guider reported the highest number of cases. Although the caseload remains low, the high case fatality rate may indicate delays in detection and referral or limited access to quality case management.

Continued surveillance, WASH interventions, risk communication and community engagement and cross-border coordination remain critical to prevent further spread and reduce mortality

fields.title: UNICEF Djibouti Humanitarian Flash Update No. 3 (Refugee influx from Yemen), 7 October 2026
fields.body:
**Highlights**

- As of 7 October 2026, according to the Prefecture of Obock, 3,807 people have arrived in Djibouti from Yemen, including refugees identified in host families in Obock. 50% are children (around 1,900), and 15 per cent are children under five. Arrivals continue : 78 new arrivals were recorded between 28 September and 2 October.
- Acute watery diarrhoea (AWD) cases have been reported in Markazi village. 35 cases have been reported and children under 15 account for 74% of cases.
- The Ministry of Health leads the AWD response, and UNICEF is supporting case management, supplies, infection prevention and control (IPC) and hygiene promotion.
- UNICEF is supporting safe water and sanitation in Markazi, including water trucking, 6 water points management and 43 emergency latrines, as well as support to the national office for water and sanitation to increase water production in Obock.
- Acute malnutrition among targeted screened children is very high. Of 267 children aged 6–59 months screened, 69 had severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 97 had moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). As screening focused on children at higher risk, these results are not representative of the refugee population, but they call for urgent scale-up of treatment and infant feeding support.
- Child protection caseload is growing. Nine unaccompanied and separated children have been identified and referred to UNICEF. The UNICEF-supported child-friendly space has provides services to 330 children since 16 September.
- **UNICEF requires 3 million United States dollars (USD) to respond to the needs of children and families over six months.**

fields.title: Brazil: Floods DREF Final Report (MDRBR012)
fields.body:
**Description of the Event**

Areas affected in Minas Gerais. February, 2026.

**Date of event**

26-02-2026

**What happened, where and when?**

In February 2026, the Zona da Mata region in Minas Gerais, Brazil, suffered one of the most severe socio-environmental disasters in its recent history due to extreme rainfall. In 12 hours, accumulated precipitation reached up to 220 milimetres, representing four times the expected monthly average for the region. This phenomenon triggered flash floods and massive landslides in densely populated urban areas, primarily affecting the municipalities of Juiz de Fora and Ubá. Although the rains were seasonal, this specific event generated an exceptionally high humanitarian impact concentrated in the aforementioned zones, affecting approximately 5,510 individuals, all of whom were subsequently displaced from their homes. The disaster was officially classified as the fourth deadliest rainfall-related disaster in Brazil over the last decade, resulting in 74 confirmed deaths and leaving one person missing, whose body was ultimately recovered by 17 March.

Geographically, the impact was concentrated within specific municipal boundaries. Juiz de Fora (population 540,000) lies in the south-east of the state, near the border with Rio de Janeiro state, on the Paraibuna River, a tributary of the Paraíba do Sul. It is 272 kilometres from Belo Horizonte, the state capital. Ubá (population 103,000), also in the Zona da Mata, is 290 kilometres from Belo Horizonte. Regarding the historical context of exposure, Minas Gerais had frequently faced recurrent flooding, though the prevalence of such events was historically higher in Juiz de Fora than in Ubá. Since the year 2000, the region had recorded at least 19 relevant hydrometeorological events evenly distributed over time, with a clear predominance of pluvial flooding. Within this vulnerable context, the recent disaster pushed population risks to critical levels; in Juiz de Fora alone, an estimated 129,000 people were living in areas classified under high geological and hydrological risk. Consequently, survivors experienced severe psychosocial consequences, reporting acute anxiety, sleep disorders, and a complete loss of their sense of security after floodwaters reached heights of 1.5 metres in urban centers.

The damage inflicted upon infrastructure and public services networks was substantial, heavily compromising immediate local response capabilities.

- The damage to homes was the most severe and difficult to address. In Matias Barbosa, many families lost the temporary homes they were renting and cannot afford alternative housing due to high rental costs. Some remain in damaged properties as they have no other option. Although the return to their homes in Guaraní municipality was faster, damp and unsanitary conditions persist.
- In terms of the impact on health services, in Juiz de Fora, 11 Basic Health Units (UBS) were forced to close due to direct flooding of severe structural risks. The Emergency Hospital (Hospital de Pronto Socorro - HPS), the primary regional reference center, suffered severe flooding in its basement, which directly compromised critical care services. Other essential facilities, such as the Terezinha de Jesus Maternity Hospital and local oncology centers, also reported significant structural damage. Furthermore, the process of returning to homes that have not been properly sanitized posed health risks. Cleaning efforts relied heavily on community initiatives and limited support from local governments, and there was no evidence of any post-disaster epidemiological assessments having been carried out.

As a consequence of total soil saturation and the partial collapse of sanitation infrastructure, severe epidemiological risks were identified for the subsequent recovery phase. Public health assessments indicated an elevated risk of waterborne disease outbreaks, particularly leptospirosis, hepatitis A, and acute diarrhoeal diseases. Stagnant waters left by the receding floods created ideal conditions for the proliferation of disease-carrying mosquito vectors, compounding risks in a broader national context where chikungunya outbreaks were already active in several Brazilian states. This situation was further aggravated by the fact that Juiz de Fora served as the regional healthcare hub for the entire southeastern zone of Minas Gerais, meaning the impairment of its health network caused a severe patient overflow into the hospitals of neighboring cities.

Although it has received limited institutional attention, the emotional impact has been significant. Communities reported trauma, a recurring fear of further flooding, the loss of belongings and ongoing psychological effects, yet there were no specific psychosocial programmes in place.

- In terms of the impact on educational services, these were completely suspended across the area, and at least 15 schools were repurposed to serve as temporary shelters for displaced families who had lost their homes.
- Regarding the impact on the mobility system, transport networks collapsed as widespread road blockages and landslides isolated entire neighbourhoods, severely hindering the mobilization of emergency supplies and the critical transfer of patients toward high-complexity healthcare facilities. The destruction of access roads in rural areas prolonged the disruption to the education system.
- In terms of the impact on the livelihoods of the local population, the flood affected informal workers as well as businesses and formal sector employees, leading to loss of income, business closures, and unemployment. Juiz de Fora’s economic dependence amplified the impacts in Matias Barbosa municipality.
